detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — collectively show 8,381 pending interconnection requests totaling well over one million megawatts of planned generation and storage capacity as of late August 2026. These are projects that have asked to connect to the grid and are somewhere between early study and commissioning; they are not a count of data center demand, and the five queues use different eligibility rules and status definitions, so their megawatt totals cannot simply be added into a single national figure. What the data do show, within each operator's own scope, is the scale of investment pressure building on the grid from all sources simultaneously, in regions that overlap heavily with the country's largest data center markets.

For readers focused on AI infrastructure, the most telling signals are in storage and gas, the two fuel types that most directly shadow around-the-clock, high-density load. ERCOT, which covers Texas and its rapidly expanding data center corridor, carries 160,906 MW of storage and 76,751 MW of gas in its queue, by far the largest gas backlog of any operator in the dataset. SPP shows 53,412 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas across the south-central US, while MISO adds another 68,429 MW of storage and 30,236 MW of gas across the Midwest. CAISO's queue is smaller in raw megawatts but is 65 percent storage at 46,944 MW, a ratio that reflects California's requirement to pair new capacity with batteries. These storage volumes matter because batteries provide the rapid-response, firm-capacity role that large, always-on loads like GPU clusters require grid operators to be able to fill.

The commercial electricity sales figures, reported to EIA for June 2026 and covering states where data centers concentrate, offer a separate and imperfect proxy for actual load rather than planned capacity. Texas leads at 15,754 gigawatt-hours of commercial sales that month, followed by California at 10,025 GWh and Virginia at 7,771 GWh; Virginia's figure is notable because it represents a relatively small geographic footprint with a very high density of hyperscale campuses. Average commercial prices range from $8.66 per MWh in Texas to $27.33 in California, a spread that continues to influence where operators site new facilities and, by extension, where interconnection queues will grow fastest in coming months. Watch whether ERCOT's study cycle times lengthen as its queue, already the largest in this dataset at 440,018 MW, continues to absorb new gas and storage requests driven by load-growth forecasts from data center developers.
